item.title: Collective Tree Exploration with Predictions
item.description: arXiv:2611.17482v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study collective tree exploration with subtree-size predictions. In this problem, a team of $k$ mobile agents needs to explore an unknown rooted tree as fast as possible, and whenever a new vertex $u$ is discovered, the team receives a prediction $\hat n_u$ of the number of nodes $n_u$ in the subtree rooted at $u$. We provide algorithmic guarantees under two error measures: the maximum error $E=\max_u|\widehat n_u-n_u|$ and the multiplicative distortion $\mu = (\max_u\widehat n_u/n_u)(\max_u n_u/\widehat n_u)$. For the maximum error, we present a deterministic algorithm that explores any tree with $n$ nodes and depth $D$ in $O(\text{OPT}+E)$ rounds, where $\text{OPT} = \Theta(n/k+D)$ is the offline benchmark, and we show that there is no deterministic algorithm that admits an $O(\text{OPT})+o(E)$ guarantee. For the multiplicative distortion, we present several algorithms that induce a competitive ratio in $\widetilde O(\min\{ \sqrt\mu\log k, \mu\log\log k+\mu^{1.5} \})$, where the $\widetilde O(\cdot)$ may hide logarithmic factors in $\mu$.
item.dc:creator: Romain Cosson, Yichen Huang, Michael Mitzenmacher, Ali Vakilian

item.title: Dual-Slack Frontier Matching: Parallel Approximate Maximum-Product Matching
item.description: arXiv:2611.17502v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Maximum-product bipartite matching supports scaling and static pivot selection in sparse matrix preprocessing. We present Dual-Slack Frontier Matching (DSFM), a deterministic, shared-memory parallel algorithm for approximate maximum-product matching. Motivated by heavy matchings on small candidate supports, DSFM searches progressively exposed subgraphs ordered by fixed dual slack. Slack-ordered certified completion guarantees a perfect matching whenever one exists, or a maximum-cardinality matching with a Hall certificate otherwise. Every returned perfect matching carries an a posteriori geometric-mean quality bound; accumulated Hall obstructions can tighten this bound and improve the returned scaling. We compare DSFM with Heavy-Weight Perfect Matching (HWPM) and exact MC64 assignment on 598 nonsingular matrices. DSFM attains higher matching quality than HWPM over most quality thresholds. On a set of large instances consisting of 37 matrices, DSFM achieves a $3.53\times$ geometric-mean speedup over MC64, compared to $2.29\times$ for HWPM.
item.dc:creator: Marc A. Tunnell, Oguz Selvitopi, Xiaoye Sherry Li

item.title: Quantum Algorithm with Quadratic Speedup for 2D Pattern Matching
item.description: arXiv:2611.17541v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the problem of 2 dimensional pattern matching under Quantum Query model. Here, we are given a rectangular text $T[0..n_1-1][0..n_2-1]$ and a pattern $P[0..m_1 -1][0..m_2-1]$. We take $N = n_1n_2$ and $M = m_1m_2$ as the sizes of text and the pattern respectively (we assume $M < N$). Based upon the Quantum Advantage given by Grover's search (and subsequent D\"urr-H{\o}yer search), we create a solution which takes $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{N})$ query complexity to answer if the pattern $P$ exists in $T$. Our solution uses deterministic sampling as a primary component. As noted by earlier work in the literature, deterministic sampling is inadequate and witness tables are essential components for 2D matching. In our settings, we assume that the witness table of the pattern is precomputed classically and is available as an oracle to the quantum algorithm. Our main novel component is how to compute and employ a geometric structure called ``skyline" without losing the quantum advantage.
item.dc:creator: Rishabh Gala, Rahul Shah

item.title: Fault Tolerant Coresets
item.description: arXiv:2611.17574v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coresets are small weighted summaries of large datasets that help quickly evaluate some loss objectives on the input dataset. We mainly focus on coresets for the $k$-means objective, where the cost of the input dataset with respect to a set of $k$ centers is the sum of squared distances from each point to its closest center. A $k$-means $\varepsilon$-coreset $\Omega$ satisfies $\mathrm{cost}(P,S)=(1\pm\varepsilon)\mathrm{cost}(\Omega,S)$ for every set $S$ of $k$ centers, where $P$ denotes the input dataset. A long line of work has established near optimal $\varepsilon$-coreset size bounds for $k$-means. A key assumption in these works is that the coreset remains intact after construction. The question we ask is the following: if an adversary corrupts at most $f$ weighted entries of an $\varepsilon$-coreset, can we recover an $O(\varepsilon)$-coreset via a decoding algorithm that is given only the corrupted coreset. This models situations where entries of the coreset can be corrupted during storage or transmission, and recovery must proceed without access to the original dataset. Our main result shows that increasing the usual coreset size by an additive $O(fk/\varepsilon)$ yields a coreset that can be decoded into an $O(\varepsilon)$-coreset after any $f$ adversarial corruptions. This bound is achieved by sensitivity sampling, a widely used method for constructing coresets. Our result is optimal in the sense that any fault tolerant coreset, whose decoding algorithm only keeps a subset of the points must also have size $\Omega(fk/\varepsilon)$. Our experiments demonstrate recovery under adversarial corruptions.
item.dc:creator: Milind Prabhu, Chris Schwiegelshohn, Sudarshan Shyam

item.title: LinearKnot: Linear-Time Approximation of the Pseudoknot Partition Function
item.description: arXiv:2611.17602v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pseudoknots, where two or more helices cross, are central to many functional RNAs, including frameshifting signals, telomerase RNA, riboswitches and viral genomes. With arbitrary pseudoknots, finding the minimum free energy structure is NP-hard, so most RNA secondary structure prediction tools only consider pseudoknot-free structures. Dirks and Pierce (DP03) pioneered the first pseudoknot partition function, which underlies NUPACK's pseudoknot model, but it takes $O(n^5)$ time and $O(n^4)$ memory, making it practical only for very short sequences. Linear-time approximate dynamic programming, as in LinearFold and LinearPartition, does not transfer easily to DP03: a partial pseudoknot leaves a gap filled by its crossing partner, whose complementary sequence may still lie ahead of the scan, so it cannot be ranked by its inside weight. We present LinearKnot, a linear-time approximation of DP03 in three passes: (a) LinearPartition gives pseudoknot-free weights; (b) a second pass builds tables that estimate each partial stem's crossing partner; and (c) a third scans a left-to-right reformulation of DP03 that reserves the 5' nucleotides in the pseudoknot helix for subsequent pairing, keeping the states with the largest estimated contribution. Without pruning, this reformulation computes DP03's pseudoknot recursion exactly, so the only approximation is which states the beam keeps. End-to-end, time grows linearly ($n^{1.01}$) and memory marginally above linear ($n^{1.15}$) from 1,000 to 9,392 nt. LinearKnot folds the 9,392 nt Rous sarcoma virus genome in 2.4 hours and 90.5 GB, where exact DP03 would need an estimated 40,000 years and 54 million GB, and matches exact DP03 base-pair probabilities on 418 PseudoBase RNAs with a median RMSD of $9.2\times10^{-7}$. Our code is available at https://github.com/gautammilan/LinearKnot.
item.dc:creator: Milan Gautam, David H. Mathews, Liang Huang

item.title: Exact Failure Probabilities for d-Choice Cuckoo Hashing
item.description: arXiv:2611.17688v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In d-choice cuckoo hashing, each of n items must be placed in one of its d candidate slots in a table of M slots, and every slot holds at most one item. We give a polynomial-time dynamic programming algorithm to compute the exact probability that no valid placement exists. Our method also handles the variant with separate tables.
item.dc:creator: Chenyang Zhang, Ling Ren

item.title: Tight Quantum Query Bounds for Minimum Cut and Multicut on Dense Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2611.17845v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We determine the dense worst-case quantum query complexity of exact minimum multicut on simple unweighted undirected graphs. With at most $k$ explicit demand pairs, our adjacency-array algorithm uses $\OO(n+\min\{m,n^{3/2}\sqrt{k}\})$ queries; a matching lower bound holds for every $1\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ and sufficiently large $n$, with constants uniform in $k$. In particular, the $k=1$ case gives an $\OO(n^{3/2})$ query algorithm for prescribed $s$--$t$ cut. The upper bound combines degree-sensitive spectral estimates of local improvement with refinement by unions of label classes. These steps retain every original optimum and permit exact acquisition without an additional label-count factor. Separately, we prove an $\Omega(n^{3/2})$ global minimum-cut lower bound on dense connected graphs, matching the existing upper bound up to polylogarithmic factors. It holds for the value and for any optimum shore, even with known degrees and sorted neighbor arrays; regular hard instances have balanced optimum cuts. Both lower bounds use degree-preserving switches and classify optimum outputs across a hidden threshold. Our upper bound concerns input queries, not total running time: computation on acquired data may be exponential, even in the single-demand case. Matching bounds at each prescribed sparse edge count are not established.
item.dc:creator: Tianhang Lu, Runtian Ren, Shengcai Liu

item.title: Parameterized Approximation for Minimizing Uncovered Elements and Unsatisfied Constraints
item.description: arXiv:2611.17951v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Min-UnCoverage asks for at most $k$ sets minimizing uncovered weight. Min-Unsat SAT and Min-Unsat CSP ask for an assignment with at most $k$ true variables minimizing the weight of unsatisfied clauses or constraints. For constraints of arity at most $d$, we give a deterministic $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation for weighted Min-Unsat CSP in $(dk/\varepsilon)^{O(k)}N^{O(1)}$ time, where $N$ is the input size. This also gives approximation schemes for bounded-arity SAT and coverage with bounded element frequency. We show that weighted coverage with set size at most $d$ can be solved exactly in $2^{O(kd)}N^{O(1)}$ time by adapting color-coding. For coverage on incidence graphs of bounded semi-ladder index, we give a deterministic parameterized approximation scheme . We show that, unless $\mathrm{FPT}=\mathrm{W}[1]$, SAT and CSP have no finite-factor FPT approximation parameterized by $k+d$ when variable frequency is at most $d$, or on $K_{3,3}$-free incidence graphs of semi-ladder index at most four. Known Hitting Set hardness gives the same lower bound for all three problems at VC dimension two. Under the same assumption, we show that no computable relaxation $g(k,d)\geq k$ allows an FPT algorithm to preserve a prescribed unsatisfied-weight target for SAT or CSP, already for arity three and, separately, bounded variable frequency. For coverage, known algorithms preserve the target using at most $k+1$ sets on incidence graphs of bounded semi-ladder index.
item.dc:creator: Rudranarayan Kar, Souvik Saha, Abhishek Sahu

item.title: Long rational and Gaussian integer multiplication
item.description: arXiv:2611.18028v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long integer multiplication is a fundamental operation in computational algebra, heavily relying on Toom--Cook and related evaluation-interpolation algorithms. Conventional wisdom dictates that multiplication on the Gaussian integers $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ is reduced to standard rational integer multiplication, since $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ is a ring extension of $\mathbb{Z}$. We show that this approach is far from optimal and moreover inverting this established paradigm, that is reducing rational to Gaussian multiplication, leads to faster rational integer multiplication algorithms. We introduce a novel Toom--Cook framework that reduces rational long integer multiplication to Gaussian integer multiplication, yielding a strictly more efficient computational pipeline. By taking advantage of the special properties of the rational integer domain inside the Gaussian integers, we achieve a more favourable algebraic structure that reduces the overall arithmetic cost in every metric. To validate this theoretical shift, we provide a complete implementation of our algorithm. Benchmarks demonstrate that our approach outperforms the highly optimised GNU Multiple Precision Arithmetic Library (GMP) by up to 29\%, bridging a fundamental theoretical insight with significant practical improvements in high-performance computer algebra.
item.dc:creator: Yuval Spiizer, Raphael S. Steiner

item.title: The Complexity of Traffic Engineering in Segment Routing Networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.18152v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Segment routing is a modern variant of source routing which has recently become popular in the Internet. It allows operators to equip network packets with an additional header which specifies segments: a list of waypoints the packet needs to traverse on its way to the destination. This is reminiscent of Valiant routing in parallel computing and introduces an additional degree of freedom in traffic engineering. This flexibility can be exploited to minimize congestion in the network. This paper sheds light on the computational complexity of traffic engineering in segment routing networks. We consider two problem variants: a fixed-length variant where link weights are given and only waypoints can be chosen, and a variable-length variant where additionally the network operator can also choose the link weights, which then define the shortest paths taken between the waypoints. We prove that the first variant is NP-hard even if the network graph is planar and if all demands and link weights are 1. We also show that the second variant is NP-hard already for planar network graphs with all demands being 1. On the positive side, we present a compact and general mixed integer linear program to compute exact solutions for the first variant.
item.dc:creator: Matthias Bentert, Stefan Schmid

item.title: Exact-Quota Facility Location: A Transfer Framework and Three Approximation Guarantees
item.description: arXiv:2611.18262v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Facility location with outliers asks which facilities to open and which clients to serve, subject to a prescribed service quota. We give a framework for transferring facility-location cost certificates to this exact-quota setting. The framework yields deterministic polynomial-time approximation guarantees of $571/376<1.52$ for metric facility location with outliers, strictly less than $1.853$ for priority facility location with outliers, and $2.16995<2.17$ for squared-metric facility location with outliers. Each algorithm serves the prescribed number of clients and pays the original facility-opening costs. The framework separates initialization from improvement. A growth process is stopped when it first reaches the quota; deleting excess clients from its last batch leaves a payment deficit supported on a bounded number of facilities. Greedy additions then reoptimize the served client set. A threshold-coverage representation makes the resulting service cost supermodular and allows the usual density analysis to compare different client sets. Finally, enumerating and prepaying a constant number of expensive facilities absorbs the exceptional costs. A transfer theorem states exactly which initialization certificate is sufficient and how many prepaid facilities it requires. The three applications supply this certificate in different ways. The metric case uses a quota prefix of reassigning JMS; the priority case uses persistent contributions and a cleanup ordered by service level; and the squared-metric case uses a local factor-revealing certificate valid for arbitrary client subsets of the same run. We provide complete finite proofs of the numerical interfaces, including an exact rational certificate for the squared-metric bound.
item.dc:creator: Hang Luo

item.title: How rigid is maximum cardinality search? Stability and locality of MCS orderings under edge updates, verified in Lean
item.description: arXiv:2611.18369v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For which sets F of edge modifications do a graph G and the modified graph share a maximum cardinality search (MCS) ordering? We prove that they do whenever, along every proper common MCS prefix, each unchosen vertex's neighbour count in the second graph exceeds its count in the first by zero or one. In particular, inserting or deleting any matching, or flipping a single edge, preserves a common ordering, and under the same hypothesis every common MCS prefix extends to a full common ordering without backtracking. Neither part of the hypothesis can simply be dropped: inserting a triangle, a P_4 or a 2P_3 shows that the +1 bound cannot be relaxed to +2, and a disjoint mixed insert/delete pair shows that the one-directional condition is needed. For the canonical ordering (smallest-index tie-breaking) under a single-edge update, an insertion can first change the ordering only strictly between the endpoints' positions, and a deletion only at the later endpoint; when no break fires, the ordering is unchanged. A boolean-adjacency executable refines the abstract probe-then-repair update. All of these results, including the four obstructions, are proved in Lean 4 over Mathlib, re-checked by independent kernel checkers, and registered in the Palomar registry. On paper we further show that the first break of an insertion is located in O((deg(v)+1) log n) time, independent of the window length. We claim no worst-case asymptotic speedup over recomputation.
item.dc:creator: Md Thoriqul Islam Thonmay, Gregory Morse

item.title: A Framework for Cost-Preserving Rounding with Applications to Laminar Thin Trees
item.description: arXiv:2611.18399v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the context of finding thin trees, like laminarly-thin trees or globally-thin trees, it turned out to be challenging to round a fractional solution to an integral one without losing cost, while only having a constant-factor violation of the thinness constraints. We provide a general framework for this problem, in a much broader context, that reduces the problem to finding a certain type of rounding algorithm with only an approximate prize guarantee. We show that, up to a change in constants, the rounding problem with approximate prize guarantee that we use is equivalent to the original question. As an application, we obtain a polynomial-time algorithm that finds a laminar constantly-thin tree of cost no higher than the one of the natural linear programming solution, thus obtaining the first result without cost loss of this type (even for the special case of chain-constrained trees). Moreover, our framework gives a new perspective on how to approach the problem of finding globally-thin trees without cost loss.
item.dc:creator: Jannis Blauth, Rico Zenklusen

item.title: A Common Improved Bound for Asymmetric TSP and Path TSP
item.description: arXiv:2611.18498v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give polynomial-time $(R_*+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithms for asymmetric TSP and asymmetric path TSP, for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$, where $R_*=6+\sqrt2+\sqrt{15+6\sqrt2}\approx12.2604$. Both guarantees hold relative to the corresponding subtour relaxations, whose integrality ratios are therefore at most $R_*$. This improves the previous guarantees of below $14.7$ for asymmetric TSP and $15$ for asymmetric path TSP [Vygen, 2026]. Our algorithms strengthen subtour covers and recursive augmentation in the laminar framework [Svensson, Tarnawski, Vegh, JACM'20; Traub, Vygen, 2025]. The recursive analysis retains the paths through contracted regions and accounts jointly for their cost and the dual mass they visit. We also improve the reduction from asymmetric path TSP to vertebrate pairs [Traub, Vygen, 2025] by comparing two initial walks with complementary completion bounds. Applied to Vygen's existing vertebrate-pair algorithm, this reduction alone improves the path factor from $15$ to below $14.7$, matching his asymmetric TSP guarantee.
item.dc:creator: MohammadTaghi Hajiaghayi, Changki Yun

item.title: Tight Bounds for k-Median++ and Improved Bounds for k-Means++
item.description: arXiv:2611.18544v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The popular $k$-means++ algorithm, or $D^\ell$-sampling, is a fundamental primitive in both the theory and practice of clustering. In the bi-criteria setting, the algorithm samples $k+\Delta$ centers ($\Delta\ge0$), and its cost is compared with the optimum using $k$ centers. Despite extensive study over the past two decades, its exact approximation ratio and tight bi-criteria guarantees remain unknown. We give a unified analysis for every distance exponent $\ell>0$, every $k\ge1$, and every $\Delta\ge0$. For metric $k$-median, our bounds are tight for all $k$ and $\Delta$. Without extra centers, the exact approximation ratio is $2(1+H_{k-1})$ (also in Euclidean space), improving the previous upper bound by a factor of $2$ ($H_j$ denotes the $j$th harmonic number). This tight analysis reveals that even one extra center improves the approximation ratio by an additive $\Theta(\log\log k)$, whereas previous bounds show no improvement. For every $\ell>0$, our analysis gives upper bounds with the same dependence on $k$ and $\Delta$ as our tight bound for metric $k$-median, with leading constants depending only on $\ell$ and whether the metric is Euclidean. Beyond the improved dependence on $\Delta$, our leading constants are smaller than those in previous analyses. In particular, for the widely used Euclidean $k$-means objective, our upper bound without extra centers is $(1+\varphi)(1+H_{k-1})$, where $\varphi\approx1.618$ is the golden ratio, improving upon the previous constant of $5$. With oversampling, a constant fraction of extra centers is known to provide a constant-factor approximation. For example, with $10\%$ extra centers, our guarantee is $5.7$, compared with the best previous guarantee of $25.9$.
item.dc:creator: Haim Kaplan, David Naori

item.title: From smoothed analysis to backward error: The power of adaptive perturbations
item.description: arXiv:2611.18545v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Smoothed analysis has become a central tool in theoretical computer science, often allowing for significant improvements to worst-case running times if we settle for a solution to a small random perturbation of the problem instance. This is closely related to the classical concept of backward error in numerical analysis, which allows an algorithm to return a solution to an arbitrary perturbation of the problem. Despite the qualitative similarity of these concepts, we show that they can exhibit large quantitative differences. Notably, we prove that, while a linear system with any $n \times n$ matrix $A$ can be solved to backward error $\epsilon$ using $O(\log(n) / \epsilon)$ matrix-vector products with $A$, any algorithm that solves a random $\epsilon$-sized perturbation of $A$ requires $\Omega(n)$ matrix-vector products. This means that a useful perturbation for solving a linear system in backward error must be adaptive to the input. Interestingly, however, randomness is still essential: we show that any deterministic method that attains small backward error for all linear systems provably requires $\Omega(n)$ matrix-vector products, resulting in the first separation between randomized and deterministic algorithms in a natural computational model for solving linear systems. Finally, we show that matrix structure can significantly affect backward error complexity. For example, we show a deterministic $O(1/\epsilon)$ matrix-vector product algorithm for symmetric linear systems.
item.dc:creator: Micha{\l} Derezi\'nski, Michael W. Mahoney, Raphael A. Meyer, Christopher Musco

item.title: Adversarially Batched Online Learning
item.description: arXiv:2611.17500v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce adversarially batched online learning, where the learner may update its decision rule only at a restricted set of time steps. Equivalently, the time horizon is partitioned into batches, within which the learner must use a fixed policy. We study this model for four canonical problems: stochastic bandits, online convex optimization, prediction with expert advice, and adversarial bandits. For stochastic bandits, we identify a universal complexity measure based on relative batch growth and establish both gap-dependent and gap-independent regret bounds. We show that the multiplicative penalty relative to the standard gap-dependent complexity can grow superlinearly in batch hardness. For the remaining three, we show that the optimal regret is tightly characterized by the 2-norm of the batch-length sequence. The upper bound is achieved by a batch-oblivious learner who does not know the batch structure, via a generic adaptive doubling trick tailored to this complexity measure. In contrast, the lower bound holds even for batch-aware learners.
item.dc:creator: Mingda Qiao, Kerui Wu

item.title: Color Refinement Distinguishes Connected Rooted Outerplanar Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2611.18391v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Color refinement, also known as the $1$-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman algorithm ($1$-WL), is a classical near-linear-time heuristic for graph isomorphism, which also captures the expressive power of message-passing graph neural networks. A long line of work asks on which graph classes $1$-WL, or its higher-dimensional variant $k$-WL, identifies every graph; the least such $k$ is the WL-dimension of the class. Planar graphs have WL-dimension at most $3$ (Kiefer, Ponomarenko and Schweitzer, 2019), and whether $2$-WL already distinguishes all planar graphs is a central open problem. We bring new insight on this question for outerplanar graphs, whose WL-dimension is $2$. We show that color refinement, i.e. 1-WL, distinguishes connected rooted outerplanar graphs: two non-isomorphic such graphs receive different stable colorings once a single vertex, the root, is individualized. The root is necessary, as there are non-isomorphic $2$-connected outerplanar graphs that color refinement does not distinguish. Our result extends to pseudo-rooted graphs, in which the stable coloring merely contains a singleton color class, and to non-connected graphs whose components all contain such a class. Consequently, the $(1,1)$-WL test of Rattan and Seppelt (2023) distinguishes all outerplanar graphs. We proceed by inversion: we reconstruct a connected rooted outerplanar graph, up to isomorphism, from its color graph, the weighted quotient of the graph by its stable color classes, together with its root color. The reconstruction runs in time linear in the output size and is canonical, which yields a near-linear-time canonization algorithm for these graphs. Our main tool is a dichotomy lemma, formalized in Rocq: in a rooted outerplanar graph with an equitable coloring, every block either receives pairwise distinct colors or admits a color-preserving mirror symmetry fixing its vertex closest to the root.
item.dc:creator: Louann Coste (DI-ENS), M{\'o}nika Csik{\'o}s (IRIF), Laurent Viennot (DI-ENS, ARGO)

item.title: A Fine-Grained Classification of Subquadratic Patterns for Subgraph Listing and Friends
item.description: arXiv:2404.04369v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In an $m$-edge host graph $G$, all triangles can be listed in time $O(m^{1.5})$ [Itai, Rodeh '78], and all $k$-cycles can be listed in time $O(m^{2-1/{\lceil k/2 \rceil}} + t)$ where $t$ is the output size [Alon, Yuster, Zwick '97]. These classic results also hold for the colored problem variant, where the nodes of the host graph $G$ are colored by nodes in the pattern graph $H$, and we are only interested in subgraphs of $G$ that are isomorphic to the pattern $H$ and respect the colors. We study the problem of listing all $H$-subgraphs in the colored setting, for fixed pattern graphs $H$. As our main result, we determine all pattern graphs $H$ such that all $H$-subgraphs can be listed in subquadratic time $O(m^{2-\varepsilon} + t)$, where $t$ is the output size. Moreover, for each such subquadratic pattern $H$ we determine the smallest exponent $c(H)$ such that all $H$-subgraphs can be listed in time $O(m^{c(H)} + t)$. This is a vast generalization of the classic results on triangles and cycles. We also show the same results for two related problems: finding an $H$-subgraph of minimum total edge-weight in time $O(m^{c(H)})$, and enumerating all $H$-subgraphs in $O(m^{c(H)})$ preprocessing time and constant delay. Again we determine all pattern graphs $H$ that have complexity $c(H) < 2$, and for each such subquadratic pattern we determine the optimal complexity $c(H)$. To prove these results, we design new algorithms and prove conditional lower bounds based on standard hypotheses from fine-grained complexity theory. For our algorithms we introduce a new ingredient that we call hyper-degree splitting, where we split tuples of nodes into high degree and low degree depending on their number of common neighbors. This technique generalizes the classic high-degree-low-degree approach (which only splits along degrees of single nodes) and is crucial to obtain optimal algorithms.
item.dc:creator: Karl Bringmann, Egor Gorbachev

item.title: Random Abstract Cell Complexes
item.description: arXiv:2406.01999v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In machine learning and signal processing, methods based on (abstract) cell complexes (CCs) are being applied successfully in different applications. However, there is currently a lack of random models, which are necessary for a thorough evaluation of these methods, both by generating synthetic data and as null models to compare results to. We fill this gap by defining a random model for abstract cell complexes based on independent inclusion probabilities, similar to the Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi model for graphs. We also discuss how modifications to bias the model to incorporate more structure can be implemented. The model can also be used to lift a graph (or other cell complex) to a cell complex of arbitrary dimension. The main challenge in this is that the number of cycles (possible 2-cells) on graphs is exponential, and the same is true in higher dimensions. We overcome this complexity with an approximate sampling algorithm limited to 2-cells (polygons) that is based on a recent advance in sampling cycles on a graph. Using this algorithm, we analyze the properties of random 2-dimensional CCs and showcase its usage as a performance baseline for both topological signal processing and topological deep learning. The algorithm is available in the package py-raccoon on the Python Package Index.
item.dc:creator: Josef Hoppe, Michael T. Schaub

item.title: Adaptive Power Iteration Method for Differentially Private PCA
item.description: arXiv:2602.11454v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study $\left(\epsilon,\delta\right)$-differentially private algorithms for the problem of approximately computing the top singular vector of a matrix $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ where each row of $A$ is a data point in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$. Following Dwork-Talwar-Thakurta-Zhang (STOC 2014), we consider the privacy model where neighboring inputs differ by one single row. We give a novel algorithm that achieves beyond-worst-case guarantees for input matrices with low coherence, which is a structural property of matrices in many applications, including but not limited to i.i.d. data. Our algorithm contributes to the extensive literature on private power iteration methods, where we introduce a new filtering technique which adapts to this coherence parameter. Our work departs from and complements the work by Hardt-Roth (STOC 2013) which achieves beyond-worst-case guarantees for the more restrictive privacy model where neighboring inputs differ in one single entry by at most 1.
item.dc:creator: Ta Duy Nguyen, Alina Ene, Huy Le Nguyen

item.title: Polynomial-time computation of $\ell_p$-contraction fixed points for even $p$
item.description: arXiv:2607.23863v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We give a $\text{poly}(d, p, \log(1/\epsilon))$-time algorithm that computes an $\epsilon$-approximate fixed point of any $\ell_p$-nonexpansive map $f : \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{X}$, where $\mathcal{X} \subset \mathbb R^d$ is a convex compact set and $p$ is an even integer. This is the first algorithm with $\text{poly}(d, \log(1/\epsilon))$ runtime for any fixed $p \ne 2$. Our techniques are based on a computationally efficient version of Sion's theorem for non-compact minmax problems, and extend to more general total search problems that admit low-degree polynomial potentials.
item.dc:creator: Constantinos Daskalakis, Gabriele Farina, Brian Hu Zhang

item.title: Online Nonconvex Decision Making with Approximate Oracles
item.description: arXiv:2211.03997v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study online decision making with possibly nonconvex (for example, combinatorial or integer) local feasible sets and convex long-term constraints. At each period, a decision maker selects a local action to maximize cumulative reward while ensuring that the sequence of actions satisfies the global constraints in the long term. It is known that $O(\sqrt{T})$ long-term constraint violation and $O(\sqrt{T})$ reward regret are achievable if given access to a local optimization oracle that exactly solves optimization problems over each local feasible set. Instead of requiring exact optimization over each local feasible set, we assume access to an approximate local optimization oracle that permits optimization errors quantified by two parameters $(\delta_+,\delta_\times)$. We develop an approximate online dual mirror descent algorithm and show that its guarantees depend on a feasibility slack parameter $\underline d$, which measures the compatibility between local feasible sets and the long-term constraint. Under the standard random permutation model, when $\delta_+=O(1)$, $\delta_\times<\underline d$ and $\underline d-\delta_\times=\Omega(1)$, the algorithm achieves $O(\sqrt T)$ long-term constraint violation and reward regret up to $O\bigl(\sqrt T+\delta_\times T\bigr)+\delta_+ T$. We also show a matching limitation: when $\delta_+=0$ and $\delta_\times>\underline d$, no online algorithm relying on such approximate oracle outputs can guarantee sublinear long-term constraint violation in general.
item.dc:creator: Rui Chen, Oktay Gunluk, Andrea Lodi, Guanyi Wang

item.title: Quantum Channel Testing in Average-Case Distance
item.description: arXiv:2409.12566v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the complexity of testing properties of quantum channels. First, we show that testing identity to any channel $\mathcal N: \mathbb C^{d_{\mathrm{in}} \times d_{\mathrm{in}}} \to \mathbb C^{d_{\mathrm{out}} \times d_{\mathrm{out}}}$ in diamond norm distance requires $\Omega(\sqrt{d_{\mathrm{in}}} / \varepsilon)$ queries, even in the strongest algorithmic model that admits ancillae, coherence, and adaptivity. This is due to the worst-case nature of the distance induced by the diamond norm. Motivated by this limitation and other theoretical and practical applications, we introduce an average-case analogue of the diamond norm, which we call the average-case imitation diamond (ACID) norm. In the weakest algorithmic model without ancillae, coherence, or adaptivity, we prove that testing identity to certain types of channels in ACID distance can be done with complexity independent of the dimensions of the channel, while for other types of channels the complexity depends on both the input and output dimensions. Building on previous work, we also show that identity to any fixed channel can be tested with $\tilde O(d_{\mathrm{in}} d_{\mathrm{out}}^{3/2} / \varepsilon^2)$ queries in ACID distance and $\tilde O(d_{\mathrm{in}}^2 d_{\mathrm{out}}^{3/2} / \varepsilon^2)$ queries in diamond distance in this model. Finally, we prove tight bounds on the complexity of channel tomography in ACID distance.
item.dc:creator: Gregory Rosenthal, Hugo Aaronson, Sathyawageeswar Subramanian, Animesh Datta, Tom Gur

item.title: On the Parameterized Complexity of Grundy Domination and Zero Forcing Problems
item.description: arXiv:2508.18104v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We consider two different problem families that deal with domination in graphs. On the one hand, we focus on dominating sequences. In such a sequence, every vertex dominates some vertex of the graph that was not dominated by any earlier vertex in the sequence. The problem of finding the longest dominating sequence is known as $\mathsf{Grundy~Domination}$. Depending on whether the closed or the open neighborhoods are used for domination, there are three other versions of this problem: $\mathsf{Grundy~Total~Domination}$, $\mathsf{L\text{-}Grundy~Domination}$, and $\mathsf{Z\text{-}Grundy~Domination}$. We show that all four problem variants are $\mathsf{W[1]}$-complete when parameterized by the solution size. On the other hand, we consider the family of zero forcing problems which form the parametric duals of the Grundy domination problems. In these problems, one looks for the smallest set of vertices initially colored blue such that certain color change rules are able to color all other vertices blue. It has been shown that the dual of $\mathsf{Z\text{-}Grundy~Domination}$, known as $\mathsf{Zero~Forcing~Set}$, is in $\mathsf{FPT}$ when parameterized by the treewidth or the solution size. We extend the treewidth result to the other three variants of zero forcing and their respective Grundy domination problems. Our algorithm also implies an $\mathsf{FPT}$ algorithm for $\mathsf{Grundy~Domination}$ when parameterized by the number of vertices that are not in the dominating sequence. In contrast, we show that $\mathsf{L\text{-}Grundy~Domination}$ is $\mathsf{W[1]}$-hard for that parameter.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Journal of Computer and System Sciences 164, Article 103875 (2027)
item.dc:creator: Robert Scheffler

item.title: Listing Even Cycles Faster than the Submodular-Width Barrier
item.description: arXiv:2605.30564v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A classic result of Alon, Yuster, and Zwick (AYZ, Algorithmica 1997) shows that all $2k$-cycles in an $m$-edge graph can be listed in $\tilde O(m^{2-1/k}+t)$ time, where $t$ is the output size. This bound underlies the {\em submodular width} of Marx (JACM 2013) and the PANDA framework of Abo Khamis, Ngo, and Suciu (PODS 2017), which extend AYZ to arbitrary conjunctive queries with degree constraints. A central open question is whether combinatorial algorithms can beat the submodular-width barrier. Bringmann and Gorbachev (STOC 2025) gave lower-bound evidence that submodular width may be optimal for general conjunctive queries under combinatorial algorithms. The picture changes for $2k$-cycles on undirected graphs, whose queries have self-joins and symmetric EDBs: recent works improve on AYZ for even-cycle detection and listing. Pinning down the complexity of $C_{2k}$-detection and listing is thus a natural step toward overcoming the submodular-width barrier for such queries. For detection, Dahlgaard, Knudsen, and St{\"o}ckel (STOC 2017) solved $C_{2k}$-detection in $\tilde O(m^{2k/(k+1)})$ time. Listing is harder. Jin and Xu (STOC 2023), and independently Abboud, Khoury, Leibowitz, and Safier (FSTTCS 2023), listed 4-cycles in $\tilde O(m^{4/3}+t)$ time; Vassilevska~Williams and Westover (ITCS 2025) listed 6-cycles in $\tilde O(m^{8/5}+t)$ time, improving the AYZ bounds of $\tilde O(m^{3/2})$ and $\tilde O(m^{5/3})$. The general case has remained open for 30 years. Building on these works, we list $2k$-cycles in $\tilde O(m^{(2k^2-k+1)/(k^2+1)}+t)$ time, improving AYZ for every $k\geq 3$. The key ingredient is an \emph{asymmetric supersaturation} result for even cycles. Our algorithms use only join and project operators over multiple tree-decomposition plans, making them naturally implementable in database systems, in contrast to prior BFS-based graph approaches.
item.dc:creator: Vasileios Nakos, Hung Q. Ngo, Andreas Panayi

item.title: Express Language Modeling
item.description: arXiv:2606.10944v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We introduce a new tool, Express, for converting a non-causal attention approximation into a causal approximation with matching approximation guarantees. When combined with the state-of-the-art Thinformer approximation, Express improves upon the best known causal attention guarantees, delivering $\log^{3/2}(n)/s$ approximation error with only $O(s)$ memory and $O(s^2 \log^2(n))$ compression overhead for a sequence of length $n$. We pair these developments with an efficient I/O-aware Triton implementation, demonstrate substantial speedups over FlashAttention 2, and use Express to overcome four resource bottlenecks in the language modeling pipeline: long-context prefill, KV cache compression, long-form memory-constrained decoding, and long-form compute-constrained decoding.
item.dc:creator: Albert Gong, Annabelle Michael Carrell, Raaz Dwivedi, Lester Mackey

item.title: Online Fair Division Meets Reordering Buffers
item.description: arXiv:2607.01159v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the online fair division of indivisible mixed manna among agents with additive valuation functions. Under the standard online model, at each time step an indivisible item arrives; each agent may assign it a positive, negative, or zero value, and it must be irrevocably allocated, before the arrival of the next item. At the same time, we also wish to maintain some fairness guarantee, and in this work we focus on envy-freeness (EF) and one of its most prominent relaxations, envy-freeness up to one item (EF1). Given the strong negative and the scarce positive results for this problem without additional assumptions, we augment our algorithms with buffers that can store and rearrange a limited number of items. This setting interpolates naturally between the fully online case (no buffer) and the fully offline case (a buffer large enough to hold all items). We show that algorithms equipped with reasonably sized buffers can achieve strong guarantees for personalized $k$-value instances, i.e., instances in which each agent assigns at most $k$ distinct values to items. In particular, we construct allocations that are EF1 at every time step and EF at most time steps, using a buffer of size linear in $k$ and in the number of agents. Our approach relies on novel combinatorial arguments and on constructing a sequence of envy-free matchings that allocates most items. Finally, we extend our results to general additive valuation functions, with a dependence on the largest per-agent ratio between two values of the same sign, and we also identify limitations of our approach via impossibility results on the use of buffers with smaller size.
item.dc:creator: Georgios Amanatidis, Giulio Giaconi, Evangelos Markakis, Nicos Protopapas
